High quality training for aspiring teachers would combine mastery of content and child development with a one-year residency alongside a master teacher. High-performing countries provide public funding to address this need. We need to make the same investment here.
We also need dedicated time weekly for teachers to meet in teams to improve their work. When teachers don’t examine students’ work together and discuss how to improve their teaching, they stop growing. When teachers stop growing, classrooms become dead zones where everyone is watching the clock. In contrast, when educators are actively learning with their colleagues, they understand their students more deeply, they hone lessons in response to their students’ needs and they bring that lively thinking into their classrooms.
We must change the tests, too. Our current assessments still prioritize rote learning. If we want our children to use their minds well, our assessments must send a different signal to educators. Through the Smarter Balanced consortium, California and other states have developed assessments that adapt to students’ levels and include assignments where students apply their knowledge to real-world problems. Here in New York, the state has granted waivers to a group of high schools where students defend research papers and scientific experiments in lieu of state exams. New York should examine both models closely before it spends millions more on new tests.
Finally, principals need the power to evaluate their teachers. It makes no sense to trust principals with the safety and educational future of children every day but refuse to allow them to fully supervise their teachers. School leaders need support to help teachers learn and the authority to act when teachers aren’t succeeding. We must stop constraining them with rigid mandates.
We can’t regulate our way to higher teacher quality, but we can teach our way there.

Bob and Mike Bryan closed a chapter of
United States Open
history on Tuesday by playing the final scheduled match at Louis Armstrong Stadium.
The stadium — which hosted its first Open match the year the Bryans were born, 1978 — will be torn down and replaced for the 2018 tournament.
The Bryans, five-time United States Open champions and the face of men’s doubles, may have marked another milestone: the end of their dominant run.
To the dismay of the Armstrong crowd, eighth-seeded Feliciano López and Marc López of Spain defeated the third-seeded Bryans, 7-6 (2), 4-6, 6-3, for the second time at a major tournament this season. The Lópezes, who are not related, also beat the Bryans, who are identical twins, in the
French Open
final.
This quarterfinal loss ensured the Bryans would finish a second consecutive year without a Grand Slam title. They had won at least one major from 2005 to 2014.
Advertisement
Continue reading the main story
“It’s frustrating not walking away with a Slam this year,” Mike Bryan said.
The Bryans were on serve at 3-4, 15-0 in the final set when rain stopped play. When they returned, they built a 40-0 lead but then lost five consecutive points to drop serve. They failed to convert two break points in the final game.
Together, the Bryans own a record 16 Grand Slam men’s doubles titles, 112 ATP Tour titles and an Olympic gold medal. Each has been ranked No. 1 in doubles.
In 2013, the Bryans came within two matches of winning all four majors. But they have captured only one major title in their last 13 Grand Slam events, their worst stretch since their maiden victory, at the 2003 French Open.
Family, age and opponents who have closed the gap have conspired to bring the Bryans down to earth.
“I’d like to say that we’re getting better, but the fact is we’re probably not,” Mike Bryan said Tuesday.
The Bryans were reflective but not resigned about the road ahead.
“I think we’ve got to be more realistic now with our expectations even though it’s not in us to lower the bar,” Bob Bryan said this week. “That’s what makes it tough. We still feel like we can dominate even though our bodies might not let us do it.”
Mike Bryan, a right-hander, pointed to 36-year-old Venus Williams as an example of a player who is not chasing No. 1 any longer but remains motivated and near the top of the sport. Bob Bryan mentioned Roger Federer.
“I don’t think Federer starts off every year now shooting for No. 1,” he said. “I think he tries to peak where he can peak. We’ll probably have to start going that route if we want to keep playing longer.”
The brothers believe they can still capture big titles. They spoke about streamlining their schedule next year, hiring a full-time traveling physiotherapist and making mental adjustments.
Advertisement
Continue reading the main story
“We’re not 22 years old when we play 7-6 in the third and just jump in a car, grab some sushi and head home,” said Bob Bryan, who is left-handed. “Now it’s ice bath, massage and stretch to get the same feeling in the body.”
Mike Bryan joked, “I get stiff sitting down at the changeover.”
After a frustrating 2015, the Bryans embarked on a more rigorous off-season training regimen and cut down their exhibitions. They skipped the Rio Olympics to minimize the wear and tear on their bodies.
Still, their results have lagged compared with previous years. Family commitments and off-court realignments have not helped.
Last month, they ended an 11-year coaching relationship with David Macpherson, who helped guide them to 15 Grand Slam victories and is taking the head coaching job at George Washington University.
Both brothers are also married. Bob Bryan has three children under age 5.
“Look, being a dad is my top priority now,” said Bob Bryan, whose second child, 2-year-old Bobby Jr., squirmed in his arms and fiddled with the microphones during Sunday’s postmatch interview. “I’m going to have to figure out ways to do that and balance it with this worldwide tour that drags you everywhere. Once it becomes too tough, we’ll shut it down.”
The Bryans may have lost a step in the backcourt and some zip on their serves, but opponents say they remain a potent force, with catlike reflexes at the net.
“They are not winning as much as before, but they are still very competitive,” said Nicolas Mahut, 34, who won the men’s doubles title at Wimbledon in July with Pierre-Hugues Herbert. (They are the top-seeded pair in New York.)
The Bryans’ 2016 season has hardly been a flop.
They have won three titles and reached the quarterfinals at Wimbledon and the United States Open, and they were runners-up at Roland Garros.
Advertisement
Continue reading the main story
They entered the United States Open second in the points race for the year-end No. 1 ranking, although it will be hard for them to catch Mahut and Herbert if those two win the tournament.
The Bryans said they had been working with their new coach, Dusan Vemic, on ending points quicker. Vemic, a former pro, traveled with Novak Djokovic’s team for several years and joined up with the Bryans last month.
“One of his big things is focusing on the first three shots of every point,” Bob Bryan said. “We don’t want to be running around like we used to.”
Eric Butorac, a veteran doubles specialist who ended his career this week in New York, said other tactical adjustments could help, like playing more I-formation on serve. In that configuration, the person at net crouches near the center service line and can move to either side to pick off returns.
“They relied so many years on their athleticism and keeping one more ball in play,” Butorac said.
The Bryans do not feel as if a younger set of characters has passed them by. That is frustrating, Bob Bryan said, but it gives them hope for a rebound.
“It’s a lot of the same faces,” he said.
Last year, they almost finished No. 1, falling in the semifinals of the season-ending ATP World Tour Finals with a chance to seal the top ranking.
The brothers said they planned to reassess their season in the next few days and again at the end of the year. They are aiming for a strong fall when the tour swings to Asia, and they do not have any thoughts of retirement.
“There’s no end in sight yet,” Mike Bryan said. “We’re going to keep the foot on the gas here.”
